I.intro: No chronicle claims to know how the first people came to Dia-thìr. Ask, and the answer is doctrine, not history: cha do thàinig sinn — bha sinn ann, "we did not come — we were here."

events.title: The crack in the stone
events.body: A mason splitting rock for a well breaks into a vein of coal that shows every colour. That night lightning strikes the broken vein and it catches fire; he carries the fire home, the first fire of the Dia-thìrich. Year 1 of the Vein Era. The making of the world before it is told in the Telling of the Making (Caoran and the seven coals).

events.title: The First Canoe
events.body: A suppressed, half-remembered voyaging fragment survives among coastal Tuathaich families: a named steersman, a first crossing, dismissed by the Dia-thìrich priesthood as superstition.

events.title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted
events.body: Old sailors speak of a vast creature inhabiting the waters off the northwestern coast. No wreck has ever been recovered to prove it wrong.

events.title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine
events.body: Inscriptions in the Doire uaine hills describe something that walked without breathing, and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight.

events.title: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside
events.body: A forest is marked sacred, long before any organized faith claims it formally — the trees simply understood, the old telling goes, before the people did.

events.title: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed
events.body: A second forest, older-feeling than the first, is never settled, never logged, never fully mapped.

events.title: The Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned
events.body: An outpost, already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin, predates every known Dia-thìrian settlement pattern. No one knows who built it.

events.title: The Làrach an Dùin abandoned
events.body: A fortress in the same condition and the same mystery. Whether it belonged to the same builders as the outpost has never been settled.

events.title: The Làrach an Teampaill abandoned
events.body: A temple older than any recorded religion, its altar oriented toward the central mountains rather than the sea — toward the vein, not the horizon.

events.title: Carragh Cnoc bheag raised
events.body: A standing stone, later found carved with four words: Bha teine sa chloich — "there was fire in the stone."

events.title: Colbh Cnoc chiar raised
events.body: A second stone carries only two words: Cuimhnich an teine — "remember the fire." No one has ever explained the imperative.

events.title: Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised
events.body: A third stone carries the doctrine itself, complete: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be here.

events.title: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated
events.body: A necropolis grows around a site nobody remembers consecrating. Its oldest graves are older than its oldest legible names.

events.title: The panther roads
events.body: A migratory instinct in the island's great cats is first recorded — routes crossing the mountains at fixed intervals, for reasons no naturalist has explained.

events.title: The first named storm
events.body: A tempest severe enough to be given a name in the oldest surviving oral king-lists — the name itself lost, only the fact of it surviving.

events.title: The counting of the dead begins
events.body: The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, also began keeping count of its own losses — record-keeping as instinct, before there was a Dia-thìrich people to inherit it.

events.title: The unlit hearth
events.body: A single dwelling, preserved by chance in the island's peat, shows a hearth never lit — the earliest evidence that someone here once chose not to burn something they easily could have.

events.title: The first tide-count
events.body: Someone begins marking the high-water line against a fixed rock, for reasons never recorded, in intervals later scholars recognize as suspiciously regular for a purely practical fisherman's habit.

events.title: The naming of the wind directions
events.body: The eight-point wind system every later Dia-thìrich sailor still uses is fixed in this period, with names that translate awkwardly and have simply never been replaced.

events.title: The first forbidden marriage
events.body: A union between two lineages is refused for reasons no surviving text explains — the earliest evidence that Dia-thìrian society organized itself by bloodline before it had any coal-caste reason to.

events.title: The stone that would not break
events.body: A second attempt to open a new vein elsewhere on the island fails entirely — ordinary rock, nothing beneath it. The first confirmation that the vein under the mountain is not a rule, but an exception.

events.title: The first shared meal law
events.body: An unwritten custom, later formalized, requiring any household with surplus food to share it before a storm season — the earliest form of the communal obligation later ages will lean on more heavily than they admit.

II.intro: The people who found the vein call themselves, in their own tongue, Dia-thìrich. For centuries they treat the coal the way jade was treated, not gold: burned in small measured quantities, never mass-excavated, never anything but sacred. In this age, nobody bonds with it. The power this story knows as coal-touched does not exist yet.

events.title: The Binding of the First Flame
events.body: A formal custodianship is declared over the vein — the first Dia-thìrian institution recognizable as a religious-political order, centuries before anything like a king.

events.title: Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach established
events.body: The island's oldest continuous folk tradition takes shape: reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season.

events.title: Allt an Àigh named
events.body: A stream said to grant fortune to anyone who drinks from it during a particular phase of the moon becomes a site of pilgrimage that has never fully stopped.

events.title: Muileann chiar founded
events.body: A silver seam is found near, but distinct from, the great vein — the island's first confirmed resource that isn't coal.

events.title: Feallsanachd an Fhèidh founded
events.body: A philosophical school forms around the question of why the vein answers some hands and not others — the first attempt to reason about the coal rather than simply revere it.

events.title: The Small-Burning Law
events.body: A custom hardens into formal rule: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the coal in a season. It holds for centuries.

events.title: The first bridges
events.body: Stone crossings begin linking the interior mining paths to the coast — ancestors of what will later be Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.

events.title: The tavern roads begin
events.body: The first waypoint houses appear along the mining roads — ancestors of Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and the rest of the circuit.

events.title: The mausoleum consecrated
events.body: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first formally recorded burial — an unclaimed necropolis becoming a claimed one.

events.title: The reverent centuries
events.body: Generation after generation mines the same modest quantity, burns the same modest quantity, and nothing about the population changes. This is the last age in which that remains true.

events.title: The first written king-list
events.body: Rulers begin to be recorded by name rather than remembered by story — a shift the later succession records will inherit directly.

events.title: The holy-wood dispute
events.body: The first recorded conflict between rival religious claims to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag — settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner.

events.title: The measuring of the vein
events.body: The first attempt to estimate how much coal the mountain holds. The estimate will prove wildly optimistic.

events.title: The apprentice-binding custom
events.body: Young Dia-thìrians are first formally bound to a master custodian of the vein for seven years before being trusted near the coal themselves — the origin of every later mining guild's structure.

events.title: The census of hands
events.body: The first attempt to count, island-wide, how many households hold a customary right to burn the coal at all — proof the reverent tradition was already being formally rationed, not simply assumed.

events.title: The founding of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh's rival school
events.body: A breakaway sect argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over in a very different form.

events.title: The first recorded famine averted
events.body: A poor mining season nearly starves three settlements before the shared-meal custom, formalized a generation earlier, holds and prevents it — the tradition's first real test.

events.title: The naming of the nine faiths' common ancestor
events.body: A single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name — the moment 'Dia-thìrian belief' stops being one thing.

events.title: The last age of even population
events.body: Chroniclers later look back and note, with some unease, that this is the final stretch of Dia-thìrian history in which no single family held meaningfully more years of life than any other.

III.intro: A group of Dia-thìrians find another land — barren of people like themselves — and volunteer to cross the water and settle it. Nothing forces them out. This is the Sundering, and it is chosen.

events.title: Land is found
events.body: Word returns of a land across open water, unpeopled by anyone resembling the Dia-thìrich. No record survives of who found it first.

events.title: The Choosing
events.body: A vote — or something the later chronicles call a vote — decides who will go. Volunteers only. No lots are drawn, no conscription recorded.

events.title: The ships are built
events.body: The island's shipwrights, used to modest coastal craft, build vessels meant to survive open water for the first time in Dia-thìrian memory.

events.title: The provisioning debate
events.body: A dispute over how much of the island's stored grain the departing ships may take nearly cancels the whole expedition. It is resolved, unrecorded how, within a season.

events.title: The Setting-Out
events.body: The volunteers depart. The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor.

events.title: Two landfalls
events.body: What fragmentary report ever returns describes two separate coasts reached, not one — the seed, in this telling, of two later peoples rather than one.

events.title: The thinning
events.body: Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing required fades across the departed's own children. By the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Dia-thìr would recognize.

events.title: The Mourning Custom
events.body: Dia-thìr formalizes a mourning rite for the departed that is not quite grief and not quite celebration — reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.

events.title: Population correction
events.body: With a portion of the coal-bonded population gone, Dia-thìrian society reorganizes around a smaller, more concentrated custodian class — the shape every later aristocracy inherits.

events.title: The empty harbor rite
events.body: A ceremony develops around the specific dock the ships departed from, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can precisely date anymore.

events.title: The second silence
events.body: A rumor of a second, smaller crossing — fewer ships, no surviving record of a destination — is neither confirmed nor denied by anything that survives.

events.title: The renaming of the west quay
events.body: The dock the ships departed from is given a new name specifically so ordinary trade could resume using the old one without the association — an early, quiet act of managed forgetting.

events.title: The first generation to never see the sea empty
events.body: Children born just after the Setting-Out grow up never having known the harbor with those particular ships in it — the exact moment departure stops being an event and starts being a fact of history.

events.title: The closing of the shipwrights' guild
events.body: With no more ocean-crossing vessels needed, the guild that built the Sundering fleet quietly dissolves — its techniques half-forgotten by the time anyone thinks to need them again.

IV.intro: Humans find their way back across the water the Dia-thìrians once crossed, and are permitted access to Dia-thìrian land. What follows is not the usual colonial pattern — greed meeting reverence. The humans who arrive don't want the coal for what it is. They can't see what it is. To them it's coal: a burnable fuel, not a worship source, and the color it glows when broken reads as ungodly, not precious.

events.title: The Crossing
events.body: Humans make landfall on Dia-thìr and are granted permission to stay — the first contact since the Sundering.

events.title: The first translation attempts
events.body: Human clerics and Dia-thìrian custodians spend a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary. Neither side's account of what was actually agreed to survives intact.

events.title: Trade begins
events.body: Early exchange is genuinely reciprocal: Dia-thìrian goods for tools and knowledge the isolated island lacks. For a few years, the arrangement looks sustainable.

events.title: The first mixed settlement
events.body: A small coastal town accepts both Dia-thìrian and human residents under a single administration — an experiment later history will not repeat.

events.title: The lighthouses proposed
events.body: Human navigators, unused to Dia-thìr's coastline, request permanent beacons. Dia-thìrich engineers agree, not yet understanding what the request will enable.

events.title: The first written treaty
events.body: Terms of the human presence are set down formally for the first time — in the humans' language only, a detail no one on the Dia-thìrian side objects to at the time.

events.title: First extraction contracts
events.body: What begins as trade curdles into arrangement: Dia-thìrian labor mines the vein at a scale no reverent tradition ever used.

events.title: The first refusal
events.body: A single mining settlement declines to sign an extraction contract. It is quietly bypassed rather than punished — for now.

events.title: The currency reform
events.body: Human coinage is introduced alongside traditional barter, ostensibly for convenience. Within a decade it is the only accepted form of payment for anything requiring imported tools.

events.title: The Small-Burning Law lapses
events.body: Centuries of measured restraint end within a single generation. No formal repeal is recorded — it simply stops being enforced once it stops being profitable to enforce.

events.title: The first mining deaths blamed on speed
events.body: A tunnel collapse, worked faster than any Dia-thìrian crew would have chosen to work it, kills eleven. It is recorded as an accident.

events.title: Mass excavation begins in earnest
events.body: The mountain is worked by the ton for the first time in Dia-thìrian history, for purposes no Dia-thìrian tradition would have chosen.

events.title: The first Dia-thìrian overseer appointed
events.body: A Dia-thìreach is given authority over other Dia-thìrian miners, answerable to human administrators — the first visible fracture within Dia-thìrian society itself, not just between it and the humans.

events.title: The Muileann chiar silver dispute
events.body: Human interests attempt to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few resources the Dia-thìrich successfully keep fully under their own control throughout this age.

events.title: The first Dia-thìrian child sent abroad
events.body: A single family, hoping to secure better treatment, sends a son to be educated in the humans' home country. He is never recorded returning.

events.title: The tithe increase
events.body: The portion of mined coal claimed by human administrators rises sharply, with no corresponding rise in what Dia-thìrian communities receive.

events.title: The first of the immortal generation
events.body: A child born into the mining camps is exposed to more raw coal across her lifetime than any Dia-thìrian in living memory — and does not age the way the people around her do. Her name is Aisling.

events.title: The condition goes unnamed
events.body: Whatever is happening to the child born two years earlier has no word yet, in any language spoken on the island. It will be decades before anyone tries to coin one.

events.title: A' Phlàigh Uaine
events.body: The Green Death moves through the mining camps — the coal dust itself is blamed, though no formal study is ever completed. Twenty-six settlements record cases.

events.title: The first work-refusal strike
events.body: An entire mining settlement halts extraction for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years prior. It ends when food supplies, controlled by human administrators, run out.

events.title: Muileann chiar expands
events.body: The silver town grows alongside the coal workings, human demand for both metals accelerating extraction the reverent tradition never would have permitted.

events.title: The second currency reform
events.body: Dia-thìrian barter goods are formally devalued against human coinage a second time, on terms set entirely by the human administration.

events.title: The five lighthouses complete
events.body: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg — the full ring of coastal beacons is finished, built to serve trade that is by now extraction in every way but name.

events.title: Gorta Baile chrom
events.body: The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, worsened by a mining workforce too depleted by mass conscription to farm its own land.

events.title: The first organized petition
events.body: Dia-thìrian custodians, for the first time acting jointly rather than settlement by settlement, submit a formal grievance to the human administration. It is not answered.

events.title: Resentment first recorded
events.body: The earliest surviving Dia-thìrich grievance texts date from this period — not yet organized resistance, but the first written acknowledgment that something has gone wrong.

events.title: Tiormachd Achadh shean
events.body: The Long Drought settles over the island's dry season for three consecutive years, straining a population already stretched thin by extraction quotas.

events.title: The first mixed-blood inheritance dispute
events.body: A legal case over whether a child of one Dia-thìrian and one human parent may inherit customary mining rights sets a precedent the administration writes entirely to its own benefit.

events.title: The night-shift order
events.body: Extraction is extended to run continuously, day and night, for the first time — the mountain given no season of rest at all.

events.title: Fionnan born
events.body: A second child manifests the same unprecedented bonding Aisling did half a century earlier. The exposure is not a one-time accident. It is an ongoing industrial condition.

events.title: The word finally coined
events.body: Facing two confirmed cases, Dia-thìrian custodians settle on a term for what's happening: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood" — rendered in the humans' tongue as coal-touched. It is meant clinically. It will outlive that intention.

events.title: The third currency reform
events.body: Traditional Dia-thìrian barter is formally abolished as legal tender entirely. Every transaction on the island now runs through human coinage.

events.title: Lorccan born
events.body: A third case, born into a mining town rather than a mining camp — proof the phenomenon has outgrown any single site.

events.title: Cian born
events.body: A fourth, within a year of the third — the closest the immortal generation comes to being born in a cluster rather than a scatter.

events.title: Scàineadh Cill ghlas
events.body: The Rending — a fault line tears open in the hills east of the capital, around Cill ghlas during a routine excavation, killing dozens and closing an entire mining district for a generation.

events.title: The first open confrontation
events.body: A mining accident, blamed by Dia-thìrian workers on human indifference to safety, becomes the first recorded violent clash between the two populations.

events.title: The second organized petition
events.body: This one includes an implicit threat rather than a plea. It is the first Dia-thìrian document the human administration bothers to respond to — with increased security, not concessions.

events.title: The taverns fortify
events.body: Roadside houses along the old mining routes begin doubling as informal militia waypoints — infrastructure quietly repurposing itself for a conflict not yet declared.

events.title: The first coordinated work stoppage
events.body: Multiple mining regions halt extraction on the same day for the first time — proof that Dia-thìrian resistance, for all its scattering, could act as one when it chose to.

events.title: Imperial overreach begins openly
events.body: Human administrators begin issuing directives with no Dia-thìrian counsel sought at all — the polite fiction of permission finally dropped.

events.title: The confiscation edict
events.body: Human authorities formally claim the right to seize any Dia-thìrian dwelling deemed necessary for extraction expansion. It is the single most-cited grievance in every surviving account of what came next.

events.title: War declared
events.body: Dia-thìrian resistance, coordinated for the first time across multiple mining regions, moves from grievance to open conflict.

events.title: The burning of the third currency's records
events.body: Rebels destroy the human administration's tithe ledgers in three separate raids — an act later chroniclers treat as symbolically decisive even though its practical effect was small.

events.title: The Severance
events.body: The war ends with the crossing itself closed. Whatever let humans reach Dia-thìr shuts. The humans still on the island are shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in its immediate wake.

V.intro: The Dia-thìrich reclaim the whole island. They do not restore the old reverent practice. The mine keeps running at the scale the occupiers built it to, because by now the extraction benefits the people holding power directly. The colonizers are gone. Their method isn't.

events.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed
events.body: Human descendants stranded by the Severance are formally settled in the island's north — a confinement, not a homecoming, though later generations will simply call it home.

events.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared
events.body: The state formally restyles itself a kingdom in form, whatever it remains in function — the same contradiction its own records still carry today.

events.title: Niall crowned
events.body: The first ruler of the restored kingdom takes the throne at Cathair dhearg — the opening name in the line the state's own chronicles keep unbroken from here forward.

events.title: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
events.body: The Great Wave strikes the southern coast without warning, devastating Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night — the first disaster the new state responds to on its own terms.

events.title: The old human coinage withdrawn
events.body: Every remaining piece of human currency is formally demonetized. A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with coal-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year.

events.title: Creideamh nan Dia-thìreach formalized
events.body: The Coal Rite becomes organized doctrine rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the coal-touched.

events.title: The first post-Severance census
events.body: The state counts its own population for the first time since reclaiming the island — and quietly notes, without further comment, exactly how few coal-touched individuals actually exist.

events.title: Creideamh nan Tuathach persists
events.body: Tuathaich communities keep their own folk-shamanic tradition alive in the north — including, quietly, the First Canoe fragment the Dia-thìrich priesthood still calls superstition.

events.title: The border wall proposed
events.body: A formal boundary between Dia-thìrich and Tuathaich territory is proposed for the first time. It is rejected — not out of principle, records suggest, but because it's considered unnecessary. The two populations are already staying apart on their own.

events.title: Extraction resumes at full scale
events.body: The mine's post-Severance yield matches, then exceeds, its colonial-era output. Nothing about the method changed. Only who profits did.

events.title: The guild system restored
events.body: The old apprentice-binding custom from the Holy Age is revived in modified form, now explicitly reserved for Dia-thìrich applicants only.

events.title: Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
events.body: A great library is established at Muileann chaol — the institution that will eventually keep the most complete surviving record of everything in this chronicle.

events.title: The first royal chronicler appointed
events.body: A formal office is created specifically to maintain the kingdom's records — the direct ancestor of the archive this very document draws from.

events.title: Fèill Muileann òg established
events.body: An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering, drawing trade from every province the state controls.

events.title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
events.body: His daughter succeeds him without contest — mortal succession within an immortal-adjacent aristocracy, unremarkable at the time, unusual in hindsight.

events.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan established
events.body: A brutal annual melee tournament begins at Ceann leathan, ostensibly a martial tradition, increasingly a release valve for a population with fewer and fewer other outlets.

events.title: Splatter and Dodge's generation born
events.body: A cluster of births in the Class-08-adjacent shunting families — the generation that will grow up to become Dubhan's closest allies, Seachran and Brean among them.

events.title: The Depletion first acknowledged
events.body: Survey reports begin quietly noting the vein's declining yield. The state does not act on them for years.

events.title: Eòghan crowned
events.body: Brìghde's reign ends young — no cause is recorded publicly. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne amid the first real succession tension the restored kingdom has faced.

events.title: Dubhan born
events.body: Born mortal, into the exact confinement the Severance created, decades after the war that closed the island to the people his line descends from.

events.title: The second post-Severance census
events.body: The gap between Dia-thìrich and Tuathaich living standards is, for the first time, measured rather than simply observed. The report is not made public.

events.title: The mine-safety reforms
events.body: New excavation rules are introduced after a smaller echo of the old Scàineadh Cill ghlas collapse. They apply to Dia-thìrich workers. Enforcement in Tuathaich-adjacent sites is inconsistent, records suggest deliberately so.

events.title: Dubhan's childhood
events.body: He grows up watching an eternally young caste hold every real advantage on an island his own ancestors were pushed to the edge of. The coal was never his to inherit.

events.title: The Feallsanachd an Fhèidh revival
events.body: The old philosophical school, dormant since the colonial period, reopens — its founding question, why the vein answers some and not others, suddenly urgent again as the vein itself starts running short.

events.title: The failed vein expansion
events.body: A costly attempt to locate a second deposit of the coloured coal elsewhere on the island turns up nothing — the same result the Holy Age's failed attempt found centuries earlier, forgotten and rediscovered the hard way.

events.title: The Depletion becomes undeniable
events.body: What was a quiet survey note in 1955 is now an open crisis. The last untouched sections of the vein are identified — and are smaller than anyone wants to admit.

events.title: Mairead crowned
events.body: Eòghan's reign ends in the same decade the Depletion becomes public knowledge — his successor inherits a kingdom whose founding resource is visibly failing for the first time in the restored era.

events.title: Dubhan begins his experiments
events.body: Early, unsuccessful attempts to synthesize a substitute fuel from mining byproducts — failures the historical record barely bothers to name.

events.title: The third post-Severance census
events.body: Population figures are published openly for the first time in Rìoghachd history — a small, symbolic transparency reform that changes nothing structurally.

events.title: The library expansion
events.body: Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings, absorbing several smaller provincial archives into one central record — the moment Dia-thìrian history starts being kept in one place instead of many.

events.title: The first working dubhan
events.body: A crude but functional synthetic fuel is produced. It is not yet an economy. It is, for now, one man's answer to a crisis the caste in power still hasn't fully faced.

events.title: Cathal crowned
events.body: Mairead's reign ends as Dubhan's early experiments are still failing more than succeeding — Cathal inherits a kingdom that doesn't yet know how close its own solution already is.

events.title: The lighthouses converted
events.body: The five coastal beacons, still running on coal-lit flame for over a century, are the first infrastructure formally converted to dubhan power.

events.title: The tavern circuit modernizes
events.body: Roadside houses along the old mining routes install dubhan lamps, ending centuries of oil-and-wick lighting in a single decade.

events.title: The word spreads before the fuel does
events.body: "Dubhan" begins appearing in common speech to mean the fuel itself, not the man, years before the economy built on it is complete.

events.title: The dubhan economy takes shape
events.body: Markets, military logistics, and shipping begin shifting wholesale to the new fuel. The coal caste, watching its own power source fail, does not object.

events.title: The fourth currency reform
events.body: Rìoghachd coinage is re-pegged to dubhan output rather than coal reserves for the first time — an economic admission, quietly made, of which resource actually runs the kingdom now.

events.title: Tuathaich resistance organizes
events.body: A cluster of northern communities refuse to fold into the new economy, continuing to work the last workable coal seams rather than trade independence for dependence on one man's fuel.

events.title: The library's Tuathaich wing proposed
events.body: A formal request to archive Tuathaich oral history alongside the official Dia-thìrich record is submitted to Leabharlann Muileann chaol. It is tabled, not rejected — and remains tabled to this day.

events.title: First skirmishes
events.body: Minor, unrecorded clashes between state enforcers and Tuathaich coal-holdouts begin — too small individually to name, together the clear runway into open war.

events.title: The mobilization order
events.body: Regiments not called to active service since the Severance itself are reformed and re-equipped, openly, months before anyone in power admits a war is coming.

events.title: Battle of Àth leathan
events.body: The first major engagement of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War. The state, already leaning on Dubhan's fuel to prop up its fading power, moves against the holdouts directly.

events.title: The wartime tithe
events.body: A temporary tax increase, justified by the war, on every dubhan transaction in the kingdom. It is never repealed once the war ends.

events.title: Battle of Muileann ghlas
events.body: The war's second and final major battle. The Tuathaich holdouts are broken within a single year's campaign — descendants of the humans once pushed to the island's edge, pushed back again, this time by a fuel one of their own invented.

events.title: An Cogadh Fada ends
events.body: Nine regiments and four fleets, still active today, were raised in this campaign; each is named for the town it is stationed in.

events.title: The dubhan monopoly completes
events.body: With the last organized resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel becomes functionally mandatory across the entire island economy.

events.title: The library's war archive sealed
events.body: Leabharlann Muileann chaol's complete Long War record is formally sealed from public access for a term of fifty years — the only sealed archive in the kingdom's history.

events.title: The reparations debate
events.body: A proposal to formally compensate Tuathaich communities for wartime losses is raised in the capital and quietly allowed to die without a vote.

events.title: The present
events.body: The coal is all but gone. The dubhan economy runs on a name that used to belong to one man. The Dia-thìrich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, and a First-Canoe memory the people who twice defeated them still call folklore.
